patient.chief_complaint: Visual aura only — no headache anymore — requesting explanation and reassurance
patient.hpi:
A 48-year-old British woman presented to the neurology outpatient clinic concerned about episodes of visual disturbance without headache that have been occurring approximately twice monthly for the past year. She has a 20-year history of migraine with visual aura and headache — typical expanding crescent of shimmering zigzag lights over 20-30 minutes followed by a right-sided throbbing headache. Over the past 12-18 months, her episodes have gradually changed: she still gets the identical visual aura, but the headache that used to follow is now absent or minimal (1-2/10) and brief. She has 2-3 'visual-only' episodes per month.

She is worried about these episodes because she read that visual disturbances in her age group without headache could be TIA or retinal artery occlusion. She is also perimenopausal — periods are now irregular (every 6-8 weeks) — and has noticed hot flushes. She wonders if the hormonal changes are connected. She has no prior TIA or stroke. She is a non-smoker, normal blood pressure, and recently had a health check which she says was 'all normal.' She is not on any hormone replacement therapy. She had her combined OCP stopped 18 years ago after her migraines were diagnosed. She currently uses paracetamol occasionally when a mild headache follows the aura. Her two adult daughters both have migraines.
pmh: No hypertension, diabetes, or cardiac disease

ground_truth.primary_diagnosis: Typical aura without headache (acephalic migraine, ICHD-3 1.2.2) — emerging perimenopausal phenotype change in established migraine with aura (G43.1); borderline LDL — lifestyle counselling

differential.key_features: Age 48 with borderline LDL; however, normal DWI; normal MRA; identical pattern to 20-year migraine aura history; gradual spreading over 20-30 min; bilateral pattern consistent with bilateral occipital CSD; no AF; normal ophthalmology
Retinal artery occlusion causes monocular visual loss (not bilateral expanding arc); normal fundoscopy with normal retinal vasculature; normal IOP
Normal MRI — no posterior mass or AVM; bilateral expanding visual phenomenon in identical pattern for 20 years; structural lesion excluded

key_reasoning_points: Acephalic migraine (typical aura without headache, ICHD-3 1.2.2) is common in perimenopausal women as the headache phase diminishes due to oestrogen decline
Secondary cause exclusion is mandatory for new-onset visual aura without headache in a 48-year-old — TIA and retinal artery occlusion must be excluded
Normal DWI, normal MRA, normal ophthalmology, and identical 20-year aura pattern provide a secure acephalic migraine diagnosis
HRT in migraine with aura: combined OCP is WHO Category 4; HRT is WHO Category 3 — less restrictive; transdermal route is preferred
Moderate difficulty: recognising the perimenopausal phenotype change and navigating the TIA vs acephalic migraine differentiation

results.title: Literature review
results.abstract:
LITERATURE SEARCH: Acephalic Migraine / Migraine Aura Without Headache

KEY FINDINGS:
1. DEFINITION: 'Typical aura without headache' (ICHD-3 code 1.2.2) — characteristic aura symptoms without subsequent headache; same aura mechanisms (CSD) but headache generation suppressed
2. EPIDEMIOLOGY: Increasingly common in perimenopausal and postmenopausal women; some women's migraines 'transform' — aura persists but headache diminishes; prevalence increases with age
3. PERIMENOPAUSE: Declining oestrogen during perimenopause can alter migraine phenotype; many women report headache component diminishing while aura persists; some experience worsening of aura frequency peri-menopausally due to oestrogen fluctuations
4. RISK: 'Visual aura only' in a woman aged >45 still requires secondary cause exclusion — TIA, retinal artery occlusion, occipital lobe pathology
5. DIAGNOSTIC REQUIREMENT: Normal DWI, normal MRA, and documentation of identical aura pattern for ≥20 years provides strong diagnosis of acephalic migraine variant
6. MANAGEMENT: No specific treatment required if aura is brief and non-disabling; consider preventive if frequency/severity concerning

CONCLUSION: This patient has 20-year history of identical visual aura — now acephalic variant emerging with perimenopause. Reassurance is appropriate after normal workup.

output.summary: Typical aura without headache (ICHD-3 1.2.2) is a recognised migraine variant; increasingly common in perimenopausal women; exclusion of secondary causes including TIA and retinal artery occlusion is required before diagnosis.

results.title: Literature review
results.abstract:
LITERATURE SEARCH: Hormone Replacement Therapy (HRT) in Perimenopausal Women with Migraine with Aura

KEY FINDINGS:
1. HRT AND MIGRAINE WITH AURA: Transdermal oestrogen (patch or gel) — WHO Category 3 (uncertain risk in migraine with aura, generally avoid or use with caution)
2. COMBINED HRT (ORAL): Oral combined HRT contains oestrogen + progestogen; some evidence of increased stroke risk — generally avoided in migraine with aura if possible
3. PROGESTOGEN-ONLY HRT: Not a typical HRT formulation; vasomotor symptoms require oestrogen
4. SAFETY PROFILE: If HRT is considered for severe menopausal symptoms, transdermal route preferred (lower thromboembolic risk than oral); lowest effective dose; shared decision making
5. CURRENT EVIDENCE: No HRT preparation is WHO Category 4 in migraine with aura (unlike combined OCP); transdermal oestrogen is relatively safer than oral combined preparations
6. RECOMMENDATION: For this patient — menopausal symptoms (hot flushes, etc.) manageable without HRT currently; if HRT required, use transdermal oestrogen patch at lowest dose with specialist input

CONCLUSION: HRT is not contraindicated (unlike combined OCP) but transdermal route preferred if symptoms severe. Discuss with GP when/if HRT considered.

output.summary: HRT is not WHO Category 4 (unlike combined OCP) in migraine with aura; if HRT is required, transdermal oestrogen is associated with lower thromboembolic risk than oral preparations; shared decision-making with the prescribing clinician is appropriate.

findings.description:
URGENT OPHTHALMOLOGY REVIEW (performed at patient's request given visual symptoms)

Indication: Bilateral visual disturbances in perimenopausal woman; visual field assessment and fundoscopy

FINDINGS: Visual acuity: 6/6 bilaterally. Colour vision: normal. Intraocular pressure: 16 mmHg right, 15 mmHg left (normal).
Fundoscopy: Normal disc margins bilaterally. No papilledema. Normal retinal vasculature — no arteriovenous nipping, no cotton wool spots, no haemorrhages. Normal cup-to-disc ratio 0.3 bilaterally.
Goldmann visual fields: Full fields bilaterally.

CONCLUSION: Normal ophthalmological examination. No retinal artery occlusion, glaucoma, or disc swelling identified. Clinical correlation recommended.

results.title: Literature review
results.abstract:
LITERATURE SEARCH: Lipid Management in Perimenopausal Women

KEY FINDINGS:
1. OESTROGEN DECLINE: Oestrogen has favourable lipid effects; its decline during menopause typically raises LDL 10-15 mg/dL
2. LIFESTYLE: Mediterranean diet, regular aerobic exercise (150 min/week), reduced saturated fat — can lower LDL 10-20%
3. STATIN THRESHOLD: LDL 132 mg/dL with no diabetes, no hypertension, no prior CVD — calculate 10-year QRISK3 to determine statin eligibility
4. QRISK3 ESTIMATE: Age 48, non-smoker, BP 124/78, no diabetes, LDL 132, no prior CVD — estimated 10-year cardiovascular risk <10%; lifestyle modification first-line

CONCLUSION: Lifestyle modification first-line for LDL 132; calculate QRISK3; statin not immediately indicated.

output.summary: Borderline elevated LDL in perimenopausal women is managed with lifestyle modification first; 10-year cardiovascular risk calculators (QRISK3) guide statin initiation decisions, with treatment generally considered at ≥10% 10-year risk in the absence of established CVD
